What makes rabbits so fascinating?

Hopping about, the rabbit is one of children's favorite animals. With long ears, soft fur, and plenty of hidden science, it's the perfect first friend for nature study.

We've gathered all kinds of stories about rabbits, including their characteristics, their ecology, and nature-study books for young children.

content.alt: Rabbit - Nature and science facts about rabbits
content.text:
Nature and science facts about rabbits

A rabbit's long ears don't just hear sounds — they also help regulate body temperature: when it's hot, the rabbit spreads its ears to release heat, and when it's cold, it folds them down. Rabbits also perform cecotrophy, re-eating part of their droppings to reabsorb nutrients, and when they sense danger they thump the ground with their hind feet to warn the others. They reproduce quickly too, giving birth to 5–10 babies at a time.

What Tangobook's «Rabbit» covers

Tangobook's «Rabbit» shows, at a child's eye level, how a rabbit forages in the meadow, rests with its family in the burrow, and adapts to the seasons as its fur turns white in winter. It vividly captures warning behavior, changes in camouflage, and the growth of baby rabbits.

content.alt: Rabbit - Great things to observe together
content.text:
Great things to observe together

Point out observation points such as the ears (temperature regulation), the fur (winter camouflage), the burrow (a maze-like home), the front teeth (gnawing hard food), and the hind feet (warning signals). It's fun to talk together about "Why are a rabbit's ears so long?" and "Why does its fur turn white in winter?"

Parent guide: extending into observation and hands-on experience

At a park or animal café, observe how a real rabbit moves its ears, nose, and hind feet. Watch it gnaw carrots and grass with its front teeth, and extend the idea of camouflage with a game of hiding a rabbit drawing on white or colored paper.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. What age is rabbit nature study best for?
A. It's well suited for ages 4–7. Because rabbits are such familiar animals, they make a great first topic for nature study.

Q. Why do rabbits eat their own droppings?
A. It's a scientific strategy to reabsorb the nutrients left in their cecotropes. It's a healthy behavior.

Q. How can we observe them at home?
A. At an animal café or park, watch how they move their ears, nose, and hind feet, and observe how they use their front teeth as they eat.
